card.hook: Most football grounds hide behind car parks. Aker Stadion sits right on the edge of the Moldefjord, wrapped in two shades of granite, glass and aluminium, and it looks great against the water and sky.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 230 m east of Aker Stadion, and face west. The stadium sits in the middle of your view with room all around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the whole stadium from here without tilting your phone up. Then try 2x or more for a tighter second shot of the granite and glass facade and the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the stadium on a lower third with sky above, and keep your phone level so the long straight lines of the building stay straight.
card.best_time: Pick a dry day when there's some light on the front of the stadium. Evening light can look warm, but check which way the building faces the sun before you pick your spot.
card.selfie_here: Head to the fjord walkway beside Aker Stadion, face the water and keep the stadium behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the building fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the fjord walkway opposite the stadium to shoot back toward it, so you and the whole building are in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the stadium from outside in the open. For matches, tours or going inside, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole stadium in one shot with a slice of fjord water at the edge, and no tilting your phone upwards.
card.good_to_know: Aker Stadion is Molde football club's home ground and opened on 18 April 1998. Kjell Kosberg designed it, and a year later it won the City Prize, a Norwegian award for building projects that improve their surroundings. Locals sometimes call it "Røkkeløkka", after the businessman who paid for most of it, and it holds a little over 11,000 spectators.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 230 m east of Aker Stadion, and face west. The stadium sits in the middle of your view with room all around it.

card.hook: Step onto Bygata and you're standing in the Molde that was lost to the 1916 fire and the 1940 bombing. The row of old town houses is the best picture in the whole park.
card.stand_here: Go to the western entrance of Bygata, the reconstructed town street at the Romsdal Museum. Face along the street, with the modern timber Krona building at the far end.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole street with Krona at the end. If it feels cramped, try 0.5x, but hold the phone level so the houses don't lean. Zoom 2x if you want to pick out Krona and the nearest house fronts.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the street up so it leads your eye to Krona, then tap the house fronts and slide to darker if the sky is bright, so the timber walls keep their colour.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the house fronts, and early or quiet hours leave the street emptier. Skip Moldejazz week (week 29), when the park is used for concerts and views can be blocked.
card.selfie_here: Bygata is the spot to go for. Walk a little way along the street, use the front camera, and keep the old houses and Krona behind your shoulder (try 0.5x to fit more in). Nobody has pinned down an exact best position, so wander and test a couple.
card.rules_and_safety: The park grounds stay open when the buildings are closed, but the historic houses are closed outside the summer season, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a picture of the street where every house is dead straight against the gridlines, with not a single stranger in it. It's harder than it sounds.
card.good_to_know: The Romsdal Museum is an open-air folk museum on the old Reknes farm. Peter Tønder Solemdal founded it in 1912, and it opened to the public in 1928. It has more than 40 buildings from the Romsdal region, dating from the 16th to the 20th centuries, and it's counted among the largest folk museums in Norway.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the western entrance of Bygata, the reconstructed town street at the Romsdal Museum. Face along the street, with the modern timber Krona building at the far end.

selfie_spots.name: Bygata, the reconstructed town street at Romsdal Museum
selfie_spots.detail: along the town street, with the Krona museum building at its far end (no page names an exact spot on the street)
selfie_spots.why: Fjord Norway lists the museum among its Molde photo stops, and its town street of pre-war houses is the most photogenic part of the grounds; pages do not say where a visitor should stand with the museum behind them, so the exact position is unconfirmed.

selfie_research.notes: Low confidence. No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with the Romsdal Museum behind them, or a spot from which a passer-by can photograph the visitor with the whole museum in frame. The only named location is the Bygata town street, which Fjord Norway and VisitNorway describe as leading to the Krona building; the pages give no standing position for the selfie. The Krona building and the town street are the museum's own named parts, and the museum is about a 10-minute walk from Molde centre, according to Fjord Norway. The Town Hall roof, Seilet Hotel, Rekneshaugen and Varden are named photo spots, but they are not places where the museum would appear behind the visitor, so I excluded them. No page I found gives rules on selfie sticks or tripods, or a safety point for this site. A follow-up search for Romsdalsmuseet pages on photography rules or a named viewpoint across from the museum could fill these gaps.

card.hook: Varden isn't a building you point at. It's a view you stand in, and that's good news for your phone. You'll get a few tries, and nobody's rushing you.
card.stand_here: Head near Vardevegen and stand about 65 m east of the subject, right at the phone icon on the map. Face west, with the marker in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and switch the gridlines on so the horizon stays level. Then tap 0.5x for the wide scene, and try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out one detail in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the part of the scene you care about most, then drag the brightness slider down a touch if the sky looks too bright.
card.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day usually flatters a wide view like this. A clear day shows the most distance.
card.selfie_here: Try the outdoor terrace of the Vardestua restaurant at the top, which is where one travel page says the view is best enjoyed. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x and hold the phone a little low and out, so the view fits in behind your shoulder. It's our best guess for a selfie spot, so take a few and see what works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand beside the stone orientation table near the Vardestua restaurant, with the Molde panorama behind them, while you pose in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: Access rules for this viewpoint aren't confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Grab one shot where you can clearly see three layers: land, water and sky. Bonus points if the horizon sits dead level on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: Varden is a viewpoint in Molde and the third stop on this map. It's a place to slow down and take in the view rather than tick off a single monument. The view and the light can change within minutes, so take a few frames.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head near Vardevegen and stand about 65 m east of the subject, right at the phone icon on the map. Face west, with the marker in front of you.

The ask-someone spot is likewise a summit feature, not a stated photo position. Some Tripadvisor listings are marked CLOSED and the cafe's hours are given as 12-6 by one review, so check opening times. An Evendo page places a 'Varden Molde Panorama' in Kvamsøy, which conflicts with the Molde location used by other sources; I disregarded it. No selfie-stick or tripod rules were found.

card.hook: The bell tower at Molde Cathedral stands on its own beside the church, as if it wanted a bit of personal space. That makes the whole scene easy to photograph, and the best view of it comes from a rose garden.
card.stand_here: Go to the little roof park on top of Molde rådhus (the town hall), which faces the cathedral across the square. Stand at the edge and face the cathedral, with the fjord and mountains behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole cathedral, the tower and a bit of fjord. Try zoom 0.5x if you want lots of roses in the foreground. Zoom 2x, if your phone has it, is good for picking out the tower and the white brick walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines, and keep a few roses along the bottom edge.
card.best_time: Bright, even daylight suits the white brick best. Any clear day when you can see the mountains behind the town will work well.
card.selfie_here: Try the small reflecting pool on the cathedral's entrance side. Use the front camera, stand by the water and let the church sit behind you. The roof rose garden at Molde rådhus is next to the cathedral too, so try a selfie there, but check on your screen that the church actually fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on Kirkebakken, the street at the foot of the cathedral steps, far enough to fit the church and its tower. You stand up on the steps with the cathedral behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working place of worship, and the town hall roof park is described as free to enter during business hours. Check the official sites before you go for opening times and any visiting rules.
card.challenge: Can you get roses, a perfectly upright tower and a slice of fjord all in one shot?
card.good_to_know: Molde Cathedral is the town's main church and the seat of the Bishop of Møre. The present church was consecrated on 8 December 1957 and became a cathedral in 1983, when the Diocese of Møre was created. The free-standing bell tower is about 60 metres tall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the little roof park on top of Molde rådhus (the town hall), which faces the cathedral across the square. Stand at the edge and face the cathedral, with the fjord and mountains behind it.

card.hook: Most buildings sit on a square. This one grabs it. The architect literally describes Teatret Vårt's home, the big granite Plassen building, as gripping the city square, and once you see it you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the city square, Gørvellplassen, and face the Plassen building, with the theatre just to the north. From here you get the whole front in one go.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole granite building and some of the square into the frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the facade, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework and the stepped seating.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up the building's long edges with them, and keep your phone level at chest height so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight suits the stone best. At dusk, try night mode and rest your phone against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the big stone building over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than usual so the building doesn't get cut off.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is an open public space, but check the official site before you go if you want to use the staircase, go inside or go up to the roof.
card.challenge: Get a shot with one tiny person on the steps or in the square, so the huge stone building looks properly huge.
card.good_to_know: Teatret Vårt is the regional theatre for Møre og Romsdal county. It was established in 1972 and is based in Molde. It also works with the annual Molde International Jazz Festival.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the city square, Gørvellplassen, and face the Plassen building, with the theatre just to the north. From here you get the whole front in one go.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with Teatret Vårt behind them, or a spot where a passer-by can frame the visitor with the whole building. Teatret Vårt shares the Plassen culture house at Gørvellplassen 1, Molde (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q11995811), and the position you gave matches that building. Pages that mention nearby features but not as selfie spots: a broad staircase on the east side of Plassen, which the crowd used at the 2012 opening (https://www.smp.no/kultur/n/B3LJ9E/plassen-pa-plass) and which the Dagbladet article describes as built for open-air staging (https://www.dagbladet.no/kultur/molde-plassen-er-klar/63212235). Also a Plassen rooftop with a view. These are unverified as selfie or photo spots, so I left them out. The Reknesparken pavilion appears in a theatre press page (https://www.teatretvart.no/om-teatret/presse/nyhetsarkiv/i-slattekarens-fotspor/), but that was a poster shoot with the Romsdal Museum behind, not a spot with Teatret Vårt in frame, so I left it out too. Fjord Norway's Molde photo-tour page (https://www.fjordnorway.com/en/inspiration/day-trips/molde/photo-tour-in-the-centre-of-molde) lists no Teatret Vårt spot. Checking the staircase and rooftop on site, or looking for local photo guides, would be the next step.

card.hook: April 1940: King Haakon VII and Crown Prince Olav shelter under a birch during a German bombing raid, and Per Bratland snaps the photo that goes around the world. You're about to stand where that story is told.
card.stand_here: Stand in Fredslunden, the Peace Grove next to the birch. The birch and its memorial are just to the north of you, so face north and let the tree sit inside the grove.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole grove, and drop to 0.5x if the trees and benches won't fit. Then try 2x or higher (depending on your phone) for the stone relief on the birch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the birch on one of the vertical lines instead of dead centre, then keep your phone level so the stone doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or on an overcast day, when the light is soft and the relief has no harsh shadows. Summer is when the birch leaves look freshest.
card.selfie_here: Try inside the Peace Grove next to the birch, near the two stone pillars at the memorial (one carries the relief of the 1940 photo). Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more in the shot, and keep the birch over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Opening arrangements are unclear, so check locally or on the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same visit: one close frame of the relief with the stone perfectly straight, and one wide frame that shows the whole grove.
card.good_to_know: The tree you see today isn't the original. The first birch was vandalised in 1981, its replacement was destroyed in the 1992 New Year storm, and King Harald V planted the third tree. The picture of the king and crown prince also inspired Nordahl Grieg's poem Kongen, and the Peace Grove was inaugurated in 1997.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Fredslunden, the Peace Grove next to the birch. The birch and its memorial are just to the north of you, so face north and let the tree sit inside the grove.

selfie_spots.why: This is the only named spot right beside the birch, so it is a candidate for a photo with the tree in view, but no page confirms it as a selfie position.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found says where visitors should stand to get the birch behind them, or where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole memorial in frame, so the ask_someone_spot is null. The Peace Grove entry is a named candidate only. Tripadvisor and VisitNorway name the Royal Birch at Glomstua, Bjørsetalleen, Molde, and the Peace Grove as beside it. The tree has been replaced several times (1982, then 1992, when King Harald planted the current one). Coordinates differ slightly between sources (about 62.7401 to 62.7403 N, 7.1273 to 7.1279 E), so check the map pin before walking. No page I found gives selfie-stick or tripod rules for this site.

card.hook: Before you snap anything at Rosepiken, give your phone's camera a quick wipe with a clean cloth. A smudge is the most common reason for a hazy picture, and it's an easy fix.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Rådhusplassen and stand about 15 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a clean shot of the whole statue and its surroundings. Then take a few steps closer and try 2x or more, depending on your phone, to pick out detail and keep the background simple. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of the surroundings in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put Rosepiken on one of the lines instead of dead centre, and if the sky looks washed out, tap Rosepiken and slide the brightness down a little.
card.best_time: Soft daylight, like morning or late afternoon, usually gives gentler shadows than midday sun. On a grey day the even light suits close-up detail.
card.selfie_here: Try the fountain edge in front of the Town Hall (Rådhuset, Rådhusplassen 1), with the statue behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so more of the scene squeezes in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the fountain, facing the statue, with Molde Domkirke (the cathedral) in the background, while you stand by the statue at the fountain edge.
card.rules_and_safety: We have no access details for this spot, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up, then pick a winner. Bonus points if nobody wanders through the frame.
card.good_to_know: Rosepiken is stop number 7 on the Molde map. It sits in front of the Town Hall in a square with a dancing fountain. We have no verified history, size or dates for it, so this card sticks to the practical side of taking the photo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Rådhusplassen and stand about 15 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.

selfie_spots.why: The pages place the statue directly in front of the Town Hall in a square with a dancing fountain, so this is the spot where the statue can sit behind a selfie. None of the pages describe this framing explicitly.
